The eleven ratings for Volex

The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo
Volex plc (VLX-GB): investment memo

Volex: a good compounder at a fair price, whose return from here must come from earnings, and whose FY2028 turns on one customer

4 November 2026. Share price 590p (29 October 2026); market value about 1.07bn GBP (about 1.4bn USD) on 181.9m shares. Next event: H1 FY2027 results on 12 November 2026, eight days from now. Money is in USD unless stated, and fiscal years end on 31 March (FY2027 is the year to March 2027). Notes on the basis of the figures are in the end notes.

#0Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line

At 590p Volex offers about +24% to September 2027 and about +51% to March 2029 at the guideline multiple, almost all of it from earnings growth. The risk/reward skew is balanced today, not unusually positive, because the largest downside sits in one customer's renewal decision.

Two events would make the skew unusually positive, and both are worth preparing for now:

Trigger 1: the price falls toward 500p on sector noise

At about 500p, with no company news, the shares would trade at 10x two-year-forward earnings on an earnings path that the company itself controls about three-quarters of.

Trigger 2: the 12 November results show cash coming back

Working capital falling and the data-centre share of the Complex Industrial Technology (CIT) segment restated would give the compounder narrative a clear runway into June 2027.

What Volex is now. Volex makes cable assemblies, harnesses and high-speed copper interconnect, with 1.24bn of revenue from five segments, 23 sites and 25 countries. Its owner-operator, Nat Rothschild, holds 25.6%, has not missed an earnings forecast since 2016, and has raised the underlying operating margin from 2% to 10.2% in ten years.

Over the last eighteen months the market re-labelled Volex as a UK AI-infrastructure play, because its data-centre revenue doubled to about 236m. On 19 October 2026 the company said three things about that data-centre revenue: it peaked in H2 FY2026; part of the gain was a windfall earned while competitors were short of components; and group revenue in H2 FY2027 will be flat on H1. The shares fell about a fifth, from the mid-October high to about 545p on 22 October, and have since recovered to 590p.

The eight things that matter.

1

The story has changed from 'AI beneficiary' to 'broad-based compounder with one exposed line', and the share price has largely followed.

The 24-month-forward P/E has compressed from 14.1x on 16 October to about 12.3x on the model's EPS at 590p. That multiple sits inside the stock's ten-year 'defendable' band (75th percentile 12.1x) and just below Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 12.57x. Much of the valuation risk carried in the September memo has therefore been spent: the multiple has already travelled about half the distance from its mid-October level to a 10x trough. The dashboard's F grade for valuation rests on the trailing P/E (14.5x, 92nd percentile), which lags the earnings recovery and should not drive the judgement.

2

The return from 590p must come from earnings growth, not from a re-rating.

At the guideline multiple, earnings growth supplies about 21 of the 24 points of return to September 2027 and about 42 of the 51 points to March 2029 (chart above). The multiple adds only about 2 points, because at 12.3x the shares already trade close to 12.57x. On the Analyst's cross-check EPS, which is after minority interests and on a higher share count, each return is about four points lower: about +19% and about +45%.

3

EPS now compounds faster than revenue and operating profit, and the market has not noticed.

From FY2022 to FY2026, three below-the-line items took about ten points a year off EPS growth relative to operating-profit growth: interest rose from 4m to 19m, the reported tax rate rose from 16% to 26%, and the share count grew by 18%. Operating profit (EBIT) compounded at 22.7% a year, but EPS at only 12.8%.

From FY2026 to FY2031 that leakage stops. Interest stays flat at about 21m; the underlying tax rate falls to 23.5%, helped by Turkey's 12.5% rate on production; and the share count is flat to lower after 3.68m shares were bought back and cancelled. EPS therefore compounds at about 13% to 15% a year, against about 9% for revenue and about 13% for EBIT.

The brokers' narrative is 'revenue growth is slowing, and operating leverage will carry EPS'. The more accurate description is 'revenue growth is slowing, operating leverage is modest, and EPS compounds at 13% to 15% because the leakage has stopped'. That description holds up better if growth disappoints, and the market is not pricing it.

4

One open driver decides FY2028: the allocation of the largest customer, which Volex neither controls nor discloses.

The largest customer (named by Jefferies as Amazon) rose from 8.0% to 18.7% of revenue in FY2026, almost exactly the size of the data-centre line, so the data-centre line is in effect one account. That account carries five vulnerabilities: its contracts run for one to two years; Volex is a secondary supplier priced 5% to 8% below tier-one suppliers; hyperscalers cap any one supplier at 60% to 70% of their spend; the 2026 to 2028 design re-award window (800V power, 1.6T interconnect, optics) is opening; and Volex has no optical capability.

The model holds data-centre revenue flat in FY2027 and grows it 5% to 7% a year after that. A 25% loss of the account at renewal takes FY2029 EPS down to consensus; a halving takes it about 20% below the model. A 1.6T win adds less (about 2 cents to FY2028 EPS and 7 cents to FY2029 EPS) than the losses remove, so the skew on FY2028 earnings is downward.

5

FY2027 is nearly locked, and the cycle of estimate upgrades is mature.

H1 FY2027 revenue is already reported at a minimum of 710m (+21.6%), and H2 is guided by a management team that habitually guides low. The model's 155m of operating profit is the top of what 'the upper end' of the 150.4m company-compiled consensus can mean.

The one fragile number over the next six months is the H2 operating margin, where three negatives coincide: the 20m to 30m one-off data-centre windfall drops out at a 25% to 30% drop-through; the premium Volex earned for delivery speed is lost at renewal; and a record copper price feeds through with a one-to-two-month lag.

Over the next six to twelve months consensus can rise by only 1% to 3% for FY2027 and not at all for FY2028. The dashboard's sell-side momentum grade (A) is at its peak and will decay to B or C by January on the arithmetic of its rolling window, even if no estimate is cut; the 86% share of Buy ratings can only fall.

6

Cash is the swing factor, and its first test is the 12 November results.

Net working capital rose to 28.4% of revenue at March 2026, from 23.7% a year earlier, because the hyperscaler's hub model keeps the customer's stock on Volex's balance sheet until the customer draws it. Finished goods rose from 74m to 118m, and cash conversion fell to 63.9%.

The model takes working capital down to 26.5% of revenue by March 2027 and to 25.5% by FY2029, which lifts free cash flow from about 46% of net income to about 60% to 66%. If working capital does not fall, EPS barely moves (about -1%, from extra interest), but the narrative turns to cash even while profit beats, and that shift is worth about one point of multiple, or about 10% of value.

The counterweight is that Volex's cash flow is counter-cyclical in a downturn: the severe case in the directors' viability statement shows a five-year cash-flow variance of only 8.1m. Free cash flow is therefore more predictable than EPS when things go wrong.

7

Management is the strongest foundation of the case; disclosure on the data-centre line is the weakest.

The strengths are an owner-operator, a decade of beating forecasts, disciplined acquisitions (12 deals at a blended 5.2x EBITDA) and a stable team. The weaknesses are all about disclosure and incentives: the data-centre line is not a reported segment; contract tenure and hub balances are undisclosed; the plateau was flagged only after the shares had re-rated on the line's growth; and the FY2026 bonus paid out in full on a working-capital measure that did not capture the hub build, which is why 28.64% of votes went against the remuneration policy in August 2026.

Volex reports half-yearly and gives no order data, so its own disclosure will confirm the thesis, or its failure, one half-year after the event. External series must carry the monitoring in between: BizLink's monthly sales, Amphenol's and TE Connectivity's quarterly results, Credo's results, Huber+Suhner's orders, hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance, and the OFC and Nvidia GTC conferences in March 2027.

8

Richard's test, an unusually positive skew, is not yet met: the skew is roughly balanced.

Favourable: delivery of FY2027; recovery of cash; the below-the-line EPS mechanics; acquisition optionality (a 500m facility, leverage of about 1.0x, and a buyback halved explicitly to fund deals); and a multiple that has already reset.

Unfavourable: the risk this memo weights most (one account at renewal) is the risk the market narrative has priced least; the shares carry a beta of 1.77 to the European data-centre theme in a risk-off market; and the next reason for upgrades (an acquisition or a 1.6T allocation) has no date.

The two triggers in the bottom line at the top of this summary are what would tip the balance.

Lifecycle

The business is broadening while the stock is stalling. The company, not the sector, decides the next phase: 12 November 2026 for cash, and November 2027 for the renewal.

Fair multiple

The guideline 12.57x is reasonable but a touch generous for a stalling phase. The Analyst's range is 12.0x to 12.6x, where the shares already trade, so the multiple neither helps nor much hinders.

The Analyst's ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: B. Foundations' Robustness: C. Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. Case Riskiness: D.

The four judgements that move the value most over one to two years

Each judgement below is sized against the model's base. For FY2028 that base is revenue of 1,554m, underlying operating profit of 172.0m (an 11.1% margin) and EPS of 0.64, on about 180m weighted shares at a 23.5% tax rate. For FY2029 it is revenue of 1,696m, operating profit of 192.9m and EPS of 0.73.

Judgement 1: the data-centre account holds its allocation

The downside branches cost 6% to 22% of EPS, while the upside branch adds only 3% to 10%. The base case holds data-centre revenue flat at about 245m in FY2027, then 257m in FY2028 and 275m in FY2029.

  • Renewal loss of 25% from H2 FY2028 (probability about 20% to 25%). Losing 64m of revenue at the data-centre line's 25% to 30% contribution margin removes 16m to 19m of operating profit a year. Half a year of that loss in FY2028 is about -8m to -9m, taking FY2028 EPS to about 0.60 (-6%). A full year in FY2029 is -16m to -19m, taking FY2029 EPS to about 0.65 (-11%), which equals consensus at 0.648. In effect, the brokers' forecasts are this memo's renewal-loss branch.
  • Design loss: the data-centre line halves from FY2029, and Volex writes down 10m to 20m of hub inventory (probability about 5%). Losing 128m of revenue removes 32m to 38m of operating profit, taking FY2029 EPS to about 0.57 (-22%) before the write-down, which would be booked as an adjusting item rather than in underlying profit. Leverage would rise to about 1.3x to 1.5x, partly offset as working capital is released.
  • 1.6T allocation win: the data-centre line grows 20% a year in FY2028 and FY2029 (probability about 20%). The ramp comes late in FY2028, adding about 2 cents (EPS 0.66); FY2029 gains about 7 cents (EPS 0.80, +10%).
  • Price sensitivity. Each 5% of data-centre price conceded without a mix offset costs about 12m to 13m of operating profit, or about 5 cents of EPS (8%).

Judgement 2: outside data centre, organic growth reaches 5.5% to 6% and the margin rises 20bp to 30bp a year

  • Non-data-centre organic growth of 2% in FY2028 instead of 5.5% (a broad industrial slowdown, with restocking ending early). FY2027 non-data-centre revenue is about 1,190m, of which KST contributes 36m, so the organic base is about 1,154m. Growth 3.5 points lower is about 40m less revenue; at a 17% to 20% decremental margin, that removes 7m to 8m of operating profit, or about 3 cents of EPS (0.61, -5%). A 20% fall in copper would cut about 25m of pass-through revenue at no profit and raise the reported margin by 15bp to 20bp, so it is about neutral for profit. The Analyst's combined branch of a slowdown plus a copper fall lands at FY2028 EPS of about 0.58.
  • The margin stalls at 10.8% rather than rising. A margin 30bp lower on FY2028 revenue of 1,554m is -4.7m of operating profit, about -2 cents of EPS. A margin 60bp lower on FY2029 revenue of 1,696m is -10m, about -4 cents (0.69, -6%).
  • Self-help earns its full value (San Luis Potosi pays back within two years, and data-centre pricing holds). The margin gains 30bp by FY2029: +5m of operating profit, about +2 cents of EPS.

Judgement 3: working capital falls from 28.4% of revenue to 26.5% by March 2027 and 25.5% by FY2029

EPS barely depends on this judgement, but the multiple does. If working capital stays at 28.4%, extra interest of about 2m cuts EPS by only about 0.8 cents (-1%). The damage comes through the multiple: one point of two-year-forward multiple on about 0.77 of two-year-forward EPS is about 58p, about 10% of the share price. Each point of revenue held in working capital ties up about 14m of cash at FY2027 revenue and about 16m at FY2028 revenue.

Judgement 4: bolt-on acquisitions resume at about 60m of spend a year from FY2028 (probability about 55% to 60% over 18 months)

No acquisitions

FY2028 EPS -0.7 cents; FY2029 EPS -2 cents (0.68, -3%); FY2031 EPS -5 cents (-6%).

Acquisitions to plan: 300m of acquired revenue by FY2030

Each 100m of acquired revenue at a 15% margin adds about 15m of operating profit, less 7m to 9m of interest: about +4% to +5% of EPS. FY2030 EPS reaches about 0.85 against the model's 0.82 (+8% on the figures of the Analyst's second sensitivity set).

Smaller mechanical sensitivities. One point of tax rate is worth about 1.3% of EPS. 100bp of interest rates on about 250m of floating-rate debt is worth about 1.3%. A 3m swing in H2 FY2027 operating profit moves FY2027 EPS by about 1.3 cents (2.4%): small for value, but large for the narrative at the 12 November and June 2027 results.

Scorecard

#1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Conclusion: the external picture has moved from 'a demand inflection plus a competitor's misfortune' to 'a supportive sector with normal competition'. That picture supports a stable level of data-centre revenue and mid-single-digit organic growth, but it works against a share-price multiple that still carries an AI label.

Evidence. The sector's demand signal is still accelerating, but competition in hyperscale copper is intensifying, and copper prices and the peso are working against Volex.

Inference. The sector tailwind is real and multi-year, but it now supports the level of Volex's data-centre revenue, not its growth. The FY2026 doubling included share that Volex captured while competitors were short of components (the company's own words), and that share is returning to competitors as supply normalises. The divergence between an accelerating sector and a plateauing Volex data-centre line is the single most important external fact.

Meanwhile, the cyclical segments (Medical, Consumer and EV) are at or past their troughs, and the restocking pulse, which typically lasts six to eighteen months, will do most of the volume work over the next year. Copper inflates FY2027 reported revenue growth by about 2.5 to 3 points at no profit, and dilutes the margin by 25bp to 30bp.

So what. Model group organic growth as high in FY2027 (about 12.6%, of which copper contributes about 3 points and restocking about 3) and about 5.5% to 6% from FY2028, with data-centre revenue flat and then growing at a single-digit rate. Treat the sector theme as a reason that a collapse in data-centre revenue is unlikely, not as a reason to expect another step up. The external tailwinds that matter for the thesis are now the dull ones: defence, nearshoring, restocking and EV re-acceleration.

Counter-case. The sector is growing so fast (data-centre IT load from 80 GW in 2025 to at least 180 GW by 2030) that even a shrinking share could mean growing data-centre revenue for Volex. Management expects next-generation 1.6T products to ramp in FY2028, and Bernstein, Nvidia and Broadcom expect copper to stay inside the rack through 2028. This counter-case is plausible, and it is why the model does not shrink the data-centre line. It does not justify the April 2026 narrative of data centre as a multi-year growth engine.

What would raise my view

  • A disclosed multi-year data-centre commitment
  • A 1.6T allocation announcement
  • The data-centre share of CIT rising again in the June 2027 results

What would lower my view

  • BizLink's monthly sales decelerating
  • Huber+Suhner's Q4 orders staying weak
  • An acceleration of co-packaged optics announced at OFC or GTC in March 2027
  • Hyperscaler 2027 capital-expenditure guidance in late January below the 'more than half' projection

Market versus my view. The brokers describe 'lumpy project activity normalising before the next ramp-up in FY2028', which assumes that Volex wins a 1.6T allocation. I agree that the level of data-centre revenue holds, but I do not assume the ramp. I also weight the sector's tier-one consolidation more heavily than the brokers do, including FIT Hon Teng's August 2026 licence from Amphenol to compete for Nvidia tray-to-tray interconnects, which shows that allocations re-open at platform changes.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Defence, nearshoring, an electronics restocking pulse and the EV and Medical recoveries support about 12.6% organic growth in FY2027 (3 points of it copper, at no profit) and 5.5% to 6% thereafter. Rising tier-one competition in hyperscale copper, Chinese harness makers, record copper and the peso take a little back, and the sector boom now supports only the level of the data-centre line. The net is a mild positive: consistent with the peer group's 53 but a touch higher for the breadth of the dull tailwinds, just below OEM International's recovering Nordic demand and above Kerry's neutral environment.

#2Internally-driven corporate change forces

Conclusion: Volex's internal change forces are strong in articulation, resourcing and track record, but they continue a ten-year programme rather than add a new force. They support the earnings path without creating a new one, and their one open leg, acquisitions, has firepower but no date.

Evidence: the plan. The April 2026 Capital Markets Day formalised the plan: 2.0bn of revenue and a 12% underlying operating margin by FY2030 (about 240m of operating profit, with 500m of the added revenue organic and 300m acquired), ROCE above 20%, and acquisitions at a 15% margin or with a clear path to it, two-year paybacks and leverage of 1.0x to 2.0x. The prior plan (1.2bn of revenue) arrived a year early. FY2026 guidance was raised twice and still beaten: revenue of 1,242.6m against 'at least 1,220m', and operating profit of 127.3m against 'at least 122m' and a pre-close compilation of 114.8m.

Evidence: resourcing against frictions. The plan is well resourced, but the frictions it has generated cluster in execution, incentives and governance.

Inference. The plan is Volex's ten-year self-help programme, scaled up and formalised, run by the same owner-operator, well articulated and well funded. Because nothing in it is new, it offers no new-leadership or new-strategy catalyst, and its effect is already in the brokers' numbers.

The substantive change since April is where the organic 500m must come from. That 500m, about 9% a year from 1,242.6m, now has to come from breadth across the segments rather than from the data-centre line, while consensus embeds only 6% to 7% a year. The frictions cluster around execution and incentives (working capital, Murat and governance details), not strategy.

So what. Rely on management for margin (+20bp to +30bp a year), for near-term profit delivery and for disciplined acquisition pricing. Do not rely on management for the data-centre line, which is the customer's decision. Treat the 300m acquired leg as a branch with a timing problem: if June 2027 passes with no deal announced, the 2.0bn target starts to read as 'approaching 2.0bn by FY2031'. The model already reaches the target about a year late, with 1,844m of revenue and an 11.7% margin in FY2030.

Counter-case. The company has delivered every plan early, and its informal tone runs above its formal guidance: '10% is a floor, not a ceiling'; an acquisition pipeline 'larger than historic averages'; and battery-storage work that Jefferies says could redefine EV margins within 18 months. A sizeable, accretive acquisition would be the most novel positive step available, and the balance sheet makes one affordable: leverage of about 1.0x leaves about 200m of room before 2.0x.

What would raise my view

  • A bolt-on at the company's historical multiples (5x to 9x EBITDA) before June 2027
  • A CEO succession plan
  • A higher working-capital weighting in the bonus

What would lower my view

  • A large, less disciplined deal to keep the 300m acquired leg on schedule
  • Another cash bonus paid on a working-capital measure that misses the hub build
  • A second governance friction at the 2027 AGM

Market versus my view. Jefferies reads the plan as credible on the record; Zeus excludes the targets from its forecasts. I sit between them. The margin target is within management's control and likely to be met. The revenue target is more demanding than its predecessor, because no demand pulse is in prospect and the acquired leg has produced one deal in four years.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. A large, well-funded self-help and M&A programme: the FY2030 plan for 2.0bn of revenue at a 12% margin, San Luis Potosi vertical integration, site closures worth about 50bp, the KST acquisition, a 2% buyback and a 500m facility, run by an owner-operator who delivered the last plan a year early. But the programme is a continuation already in the brokers' numbers, adding about 20bp to 30bp of margin a year, and the acquired leg has produced one deal in four years. The frictions in working capital, Murat and governance net some of this off, so the score sits at the peer group's 64, just below Redcare's operating-leverage pivot and above Teqnion's clean-up.

#3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Conclusion: Volex is a good business with an outstanding owner-operator. It has a footprint-and-certification moat under about half its revenue and a secondary, price-taking position in the two-fifths that the market has been paying for. Cash conversion is the weak link in an otherwise above-average financial profile.

Evidence: industry and value chain. The connector and cable industry is concentrated at the component layer and fragmented at the assembly layer, where Volex competes. At the component layer TE Connectivity holds about 17.8% of the market and Amphenol about 8.8%, and the share of the top ten has risen from 38% to 61%. The assembly layer has over 2,000 contract manufacturers in Europe alone, and Volex holds about 1% of a 140bn USD market. Volex's pricing position splits in two, as the table shows.

The hub model is the customer's power made visible. Title and obsolescence risk sit contractually with the customer, but the stock sits on Volex's balance sheet until the customer draws it, and Volex discloses no customer deposits, whereas Celestica holds 560m of deposits and Jabil 1.89bn.

Evidence: competitive advantage. Volex's advantage is footprint and speed, not technology. It builds capacity ahead of contracts, wins relocations by offering 'transfer capability as a service', and delivered data-centre capacity in FY2026 when competitors could not. In-house extrusion and moulding support about 180m of end-product revenue, certification moats protect about half the business, and Volex has a proven acquisition playbook. It has no intellectual-property moat, no optical capability and no pricing power: gross margin rose from 20.5% to 22.0% (FactSet basis) over FY2024 to FY2026 entirely through mix.

Evidence: financial profile. Returns are good and the balance sheet is strong, but cash conversion is weak.

Evidence: management. Nat Rothschild (Executive Chairman since 2015, CEO since November 2025) took revenue from 367.5m to 1,242.6m and the margin from 2.0% to 10.2%. He owns 25.6%, has never sold, is paid 1.22m GBP, and is candid ('I am not someone who drinks the AI Kool-Aid'). CFO Jon Boaden (since 2020) and Global COO John Molloy (since 2017) have never missed a forecast; five regional COOs sit beneath them, and senior turnover is negligible. The chair, Dave Webster (former CEO of ECI, a direct competitor), bought shares on appointment.

The weaknesses of management are five: no disclosed successor; the chair's second executive role; acceptance of the hub model without disclosure of its returns; a decentralised control environment, as Murat's safety record shows; and communication on the data-centre line that lagged events.

Inference. The industry gives Volex a good home in half its revenue and a contested one in the rest, and the contested part is exactly where the market focused. Volex's footprint-and-speed advantage is widening where it is mechanical (relocations, consolidation, vertical integration, acquisitions in a fragmented layer) and narrowing in hyperscale copper. The economics are those of a good, not great, business: 20% ROCE, a 10% to 11% margin rising a few tenths of a point a year, modest operating leverage, low financial leverage and weak cash conversion. Management is the strongest foundation of the case.

So what. Use segment-specific assumptions. The defended half can hold or expand its margin. The data-centre margin, the most profitable category in FY2026, should drift down as the scarcity premium fades; the mix lever that drove FY2026 is therefore gone, and the rise in the group margin slows to +20bp to +30bp a year. Trust management on profit and acquisitions, but do not read its silence on the data-centre line as a positive signal.

Counter-case. Competitors describe Volex as dominant in moulded complex harnesses. It is the licensed maker of Tesla's NACS charging coupler and, through Murat, supplies four of the five largest agricultural OEMs. Its ten-year record of beating every forecast is itself evidence of a durable advantage in execution that the structural analysis understates. On this view the right comparison is discoverIE, which raised its margin from 3.4% to 13.8% over twelve years on the same playbook and earns a 15% to 20% premium to UK Electricals.

What would raise my view

  • Evidence of design ownership in hyperscale copper: a 1.6T or active electrical cable (AEC) programme on which Volex is the primary supplier
  • A disclosed hub-deposit or minimum-commitment term

What would lower my view

  • A wider second-tier price discount at renewal
  • Another integration miss on the Murat pattern

Market versus my view. One sell-side report's summary calls Volex a 'primary component supplier'; the expert evidence (from Wistron, Google and Amphenol) says secondary. The brokers' Buy case rests on two claims. I share the first, that growth is 'highly diversified across end-markets'. The co-movement data contradicts the second, Jefferies' claim that 'data-centre exposure [is] not factored into trading multiples': Volex's R-squared to the data-centre theme basket is 40%, and its beta 1.77. The market trades Volex as a theme stock, and the brokers argue it should be valued as one. My view differs from both: value Volex as a compounder with one exposed line.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Qualitatively mixed. Management is outstanding (peer-group score 77) and certification moats protect about half of revenue. But the assembly layer is fragmented, Volex has no pricing power or intellectual property, it is a secondary, price-taking supplier in the data-centre and Consumer two-fifths, and one customer accounts for 18.7% of revenue (industry 45, advantage 47). The figures confirm a good, not great, business: ROIC of 10.9% (70th percentile) and an incremental pre-tax ROCE of about 31%, against an operating margin at the 34th percentile and free-cash-flow conversion at the 41st. That places Volex just below Indutrade's proprietary-product compounder, above Shell, and far above Solid State's one-customer design-in profile.

#4Conservatism of guidance, proactivity with the sell-side, and the record of delivery

Conclusion: guidance is a strength: deliberately conservative, specific in its medium-term building blocks, and beaten every year since 2016. FY2027 guidance is conservative by 1% to 3% on profit. But the cadence of upgrades has matured, the FY2028 bar is fair rather than low, and the record has never been tested against a sharp cut by the largest account.

Evidence: current guidance. The company guides H1 FY2027 revenue of at least 710m and a 'broadly similar' H2 (about 1,420m for the year); operating profit 'towards the upper end of market expectations', against a company-compiled consensus of 150.4m on 16 October (138.3m in August); covenant leverage of no more than about 1.2x; and a 10% margin floor. After the October update Zeus and Jefferies moved to 153m to 154m of operating profit.

Evidence: the record. Volex has missed no earnings forecast since 2016. FY2026 operating profit came in 3.0% above consensus and 10.9% above the pre-close compilation; the 650m revenue goal was reached two years early and the 1.2bn plan a year early. The CEO states the philosophy: 'all our forecasts have historically been extremely conservative, which is why we have always matched or beaten them'.

Evidence: the pace of upgrades. FY2027 EPS consensus is up 35% over twelve months, 14% over three months and 2% over one month. Upgrades after the October update were +2.5% (Zeus) and +5% to +6% (Jefferies), against double-digit upgrades in FY2026.

Evidence: two blemishes beneath the record. The company first signalled the sequential decline in data-centre revenue in a trading update issued after the shares had re-rated on that revenue. The same update disclosed that about 10m of H1 revenue had been pulled forward; the fourth quarter of FY2025 also contained an 11m pull-forward, so pull-forwards recur around site moves.

Inference. Near-term guidance is moderately conservative by habit. Historically, H2 revenue has run 10% to 13% above H1. A 'flat' H2, once the 10m pull-forward reverses and about 25m of KST revenue is added, implies an underlying sequential decline of about 1%, consistent with data-centre revenue falling while the rest of the group grows seasonally. Given the record, H2 is more likely to come in 1% to 4% above H1 than flat, and the profit guidance is more conservative than the revenue guidance.

But the cadence of raising is maturing (to the upper end of a range, not above it), and the record was built in years that each had a demand pulse and no customer above 8% of revenue. FY2028 is the first year since FY2023 with neither. Management keeps the sell-side conservative on profit, but not on the data-centre line, which is the one that matters.

So what. Use FY2027 consensus as a floor for profit, and expect a beat of 1% to 3%, not FY2026's 4% to 11%. Do not expect the first FY2028 guidance in June 2027 to be set low; expect 'in line with market expectations'. The bar for FY2028 has not been reset: all six brokers raised their estimates after October, so it was the share price, not the estimates, that rebased.

Counter-case. Zeus reports that average monthly sales in the first four months of FY2027 ran about 8% above the H2 FY2026 monthly average, even as data-centre revenue fell. The January 2026 pattern, an extra trading update on outperformance, could repeat in January 2027. Even the model's 155m may be conservative: applying FY2026's beat mechanically gives about 160m.

What would raise my view

  • 'At least the upper end' language on 12 November or in a January update

What would lower my view

  • H1 operating profit below 74m
  • Any H2 commentary implying that a data-centre renewal concession is already visible

Market versus my view. The brokers sit at 153m to 154m, and the sell-side narrative report calls further raises 'the most probable outcome'. I agree for FY2027 and disagree for FY2028, where the two active brokers' revenue forecasts (Zeus 1,488m, Jefferies 1,491m) already sit below the consensus median and the one open driver skews down.

Score: 86, set by the Rater. No earnings forecast missed since 2016: revenue beat guidance by 1.4% to 3.3% in each of FY2023 to FY2026, FY2026 guidance was raised twice and still beaten, and the 650m and 1.2bn plans arrived two years and one year early. Current guidance is conservative by habit, by about 1% to 3% on FY2027 profit. Against that, the cadence has matured to 'upper end', the data-centre plateau was disclosed only after the re-rating, and the FY2028 bar is fair rather than low. This is a record like AQ Group's, a notch above the peer group's 76, but short of RELX's guidance accuracy.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops: does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth?

Conclusion: revenue growth of about 9% does turn into EPS growth of 13% to 15%, but through flat interest, a falling tax rate and a flat share count, not through pricing or fixed-cost leverage. The operating leverage that does exist is sharper on the way down than on the way up.

Evidence: pricing. Volex has no real pricing power. Copper and PVC prices are indexed with a one-to-two-month lag; tariffs and freight pass through; programmes that miss target margins are re-priced at renewal; and volume-shortfall clauses allow price rises of up to 12% if customers under-call. In data centre, the one demonstrated premium (for delivery speed during a shortage) was temporary. The base expectation is price cuts of a few percent at each one-to-two-year renewal, partly offset by the 1.6T generation step (a 50% to 60% uplift in average selling price over 800G) if Volex wins allocations. In FY2027, pricing adds about 2.5 to 3 points to revenue (copper) and takes 25bp to 30bp off the margin, plus about 15bp for the lost speed premium.

Evidence: operating leverage. Operating leverage is modest. Staff costs were 23.1% of revenue in FY2020 and 22.6% in FY2026 while revenue tripled, so labour scales with volume; materials, the largest cost, pass through. Incremental margins were 10.3%, 11.8%, 9.5% and 13.5% in FY2023 to FY2026, against an average margin near 10%. Only the step from H1 to H2 FY2026 reached 17.2%, on data-centre mix.

Leverage is sharper on the way down. Capacity is built ahead of contracts, 81% of the workforce is under collective agreements, Turkish and Indonesian severance is costly, and the directors' own downside case assumes costs fall only 5% in a 15% revenue fall. The contribution margin before cost action is about 18% to 20% for the group and 25% to 30% on data-centre revenue; Jefferies' downside case implies a 17.5% decremental margin.

Evidence: financial leverage. Financial leverage is low. Covenant leverage will be about 1.0x at March 2027 (guided at no more than about 1.2x) against a 3.0x covenant, with net debt including leases of about 212m. Interest stays flat at about 21m while operating profit grows about 10% a year, so interest falls from about 14% of operating profit to about 9% by FY2031. A 100bp move in interest rates is worth about 1.7m of pre-tax profit (1.3% of EPS). The 500m facility costs SOFR plus 1.8% and is committed to June 2029.

Evidence: cost-out. Cost-out defends the margin rather than expanding it. Gross self-help in hand is about 12m to 19m by FY2029 (70bp to 110bp of margin): site consolidation (about 50bp, half already in the run-rate), the move from Spokane to Irvine (1m to 2m), San Luis Potosi (5m to 8m assumed, against up to 12m under the two-year payback rule), and automation and kaizen (3m to 5m). Data-centre price cuts (4m to 7m a year of revenue at near-full drop-through), Mexican and Turkish wage inflation and reinvestment absorb most of it, so only about 10bp to 20bp reaches the margin by FY2029. History agrees: from FY2022 to FY2025 the margin rose only 70bp despite site closures, Murat headcount cuts and the Shenzhen actions.

Evidence: feedback loops. Balancing loops dominate the next eighteen months, and they act on revenue growth. The reinforcing loops (nearshoring design-ins and the acquisition platform) are real but slow, sustaining about 6% organic growth and 10bp to 20bp of margin a year. The one accelerating reinforcing loop is a risk loop: concentration on one account ties capacity (the Batam plant is filled for hyperscalers), hub stock and the multiple to a single renewal.

Inference. Revenue growth does lead to outsized EPS growth, but not for the reason the market gives. A 10% revenue move shifts operating profit by only about 11% to 15% on the way up and 15% to 20% on the way down; pricing adds nothing; and cost-out nets to tenths of a point. The outsizing happens below the line. Revenue compounds at about 9%, operating profit at about 13% (the margin rises 25bp to 35bp a year, mostly from mix and absorption), and EPS at about 13% to 15%, because interest is flat, tax falls to 23.5% and the share count is flat to lower. The below-the-line leakage of FY2022 to FY2026 (about six points a year on this measure) reverses into a tailwind of one to five points a year in FY2027 to FY2028.

So what. The margin path (10.8%, 11.1%, 11.4%, 11.7% and 11.9% for FY2027 to FY2031) is well founded and does not depend on pricing. The asymmetry matters more than the leverage: a 25% cut in data-centre revenue removes 9% to 11% of operating profit, while a 25% gain adds perhaps half that, because a gain comes with price cuts and extra working capital.

Counter-case. The H2 FY2026 incremental margin of 17.2% shows what mix can do, and KST, harnesses (worth five to ten times as much as a power cord) and 1.6T products are all moves up the mix. The EBITDA margin also rises faster than the EBIT margin, because San Luis Potosi replaces bought-in margin with depreciation. Consensus depreciation and amortisation of 37.7m looks too low against capital expenditure of more than 50m, so consensus EBITDA, not EBIT, is the line most likely to be revised up.

What would raise my view

  • Gross margin holding above 23% in H2 FY2027 despite record copper
  • San Luis Potosi commissioning on schedule in FY2028

What would lower my view

  • A wider second-tier price discount at renewal
  • A move in the peso
  • Memory-component cost inflation on active cables that is not passed through

Market versus my view. Jefferies expects the margin to 'move closer to 12%' on 'enhanced operating leverage and mix'; Zeus models 11.0% to 11.2% by FY2029. I agree with Zeus on the margin and differ from both brokers on the source of EPS growth, which is below the line.

Score: 38, set by the Rater. This topic scores structure, and Volex's structure has little gearing. Materials pass through and labour scales with volume (staff costs were 23.1% of revenue in FY2020 and 22.6% in FY2026). Incremental margins of 10% to 14% sit close to the 10% average margin, real pricing power is absent, and cost-out nets to 10bp to 20bp. Decremental margins of 17% to 20% make the leverage sharper on the way down. EPS outgrows revenue by about 1.5 times, below the median company's 2 times, and mainly because flat interest, a lower tax rate and a flat share count stop the leakage: that is light financial gearing, not a reinforcing loop. The score is therefore below the ordinary mix, and below the peer groups' 56 to 62, which reflect financial strength and forecasts rather than gearing.

#6Forecast financials: growth, margins and the comparison with the past

Conclusion: the forecasts describe a business whose EPS compounds at 13% to 15% while its revenue growth halves to about 9%. The path rests on demonstrated strengths and sits within 1% of consensus on operating profit. The model's EPS lead over consensus is mostly a difference of basis; the genuine upside lies in EBITDA, cash and acquisitions.

The forecasts of record come from the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Consensus is the FactSet median of six brokers on 22 October 2026.

The model's own EPS-growth line shows +80% for FY2027, because it measures from FactSet's FY2026 base of 0.31. Against the company's 0.435, like-for-like growth is about +23% (the Analyst's cross-check gives +23.0%).

Segments. On the model every segment grows in FY2028, Medical fastest because KST contributes a full year. The company does not report segment profit, so margins can only be ranked:

  • CIT: about 424m in FY2027 and 444m in FY2028, including data centre at 245m and 257m. Consensus (431m and 455m) looks 7m and 11m too high if data-centre revenue is flat.
  • Off-Highway: about 318m and 335m, driven by defence, with copper inflating the figures.
  • Consumer: about 261m and 268m. Copper's effect is most pronounced here, and Consumer has the lowest margin.
  • EV: about 227m and 244m ('growing strongly').
  • Medical: about 205m and 238m. KST contributes about 36m and 55m at above-group margins, and the rest of the segment recovers toward a 9% margin by H2 FY2027.
  • New acquisitions: about 25m in FY2028 at about a 15% margin.

Against the past. Revenue growth halves, operating-profit growth nearly halves, EPS growth rises, and cash conversion rises by 15 to 20 points. The margin rises a little faster than before: +34bp a year in FY2026 to FY2031 (+28bp organic) against +27bp a year in FY2022 to FY2026. Free cash flow rises from about 46% of underlying net income to about 60% to 66%. Without new acquisitions, EPS grows 13.6% a year rather than about 15%.

Scope for double-digit growth. EPS grows by double digits every year to FY2031; revenue grows by double digits only in FY2027. Margins rise above past levels at about the past pace, while revenue growth runs at about half the past rate. The 12% margin target is reached only with acquisitions at margins of 15% or more: the model's organic FY2031 margin is about 11.6%.

Against consensus, like for like. The model is close to consensus on revenue and operating profit and ahead on EBITDA and EPS. The EPS lead of +5.2%, +9.7% and +12.0% for FY2027 to FY2029 is mostly a difference of basis: on a diluted, post-minority basis the organic gap shrinks to about -1% to +1% (FY2027), +1% to +3% (FY2028) and +2% to +4% (FY2029). Excluding acquisitions, the FY2028 revenue gap shrinks from +2.3% to +0.7%, and the operating-profit gaps shrink from +3.0% to +0.8% (FY2028) and from +7.4% to +1.3% (FY2029). The EBITDA gap (+1.9%, +6.0% and +10.1%) comes from higher depreciation and amortisation on the same EBIT.

The two active brokers (Zeus at 0.535, 0.587 and 0.657 for FY2027 to FY2029; Jefferies at 0.521, 0.576 and 0.630) already include the buyback, a 24% tax rate and flat interest. Canaccord pulls the FactSet median down, with 0.551 for FY2028.

The range of outcomes. FY2027 EPS lies between 0.51 and 0.56 (about plus or minus 4%, symmetrical). FY2028 EPS lies between 0.54 and 0.66 (-12% to +8%), skewed down because the downside sits in one account while the upside is spread across acquisitions, tax and cash. H1 FY2028 revenue lies between 730m and 790m (base 762m, +7%).

Market versus my view. On operating profit, the model, Zeus and Jefferies sit within about 1% of each other through FY2029 on an organic basis, because everyone works from the same guidance. The genuine differences are three: EBITDA (depreciation and amortisation); FY2028 revenue, where the active brokers sit below the median and below the model's 1,530m organic figure; and acquisitions, which no broker models.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. The measure clears 15%, so the letter is A, but the number sits at the floor of the band. FY2027's +23% includes the H1 data-centre windfall, organic EPS growth after FY2027 is about 13%, and the organic four-year figure (14.7%) falls just short of 15%. The margin rises only at about the past pace (+28bp a year organically), and the outgrowth comes from stopped below-the-line leakage rather than from operations.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over the coming six to twelve months

Conclusion: over the next six to twelve months, expect FY2027 consensus to drift up 1% to 3% and FY2028 consensus to hold. The narrative can re-anchor to 'compounder' from 12 November, but no upgrade cycle will carry the shares until an acquisition or a 1.6T allocation gives the brokers a reason.

Evidence: the sequence of events. A fixed sequence of company events will test the thesis, with external reads in between. For the H1 results on 12 November the Analyst expects operating profit of 75m to 77m (a 10.6% to 10.8% margin), working capital of about 27% of trailing revenue, net debt including leases of 200m to 215m, and possibly a restatement of the data-centre share of CIT.

Evidence: the Analyst's probabilities. FY2027 guidance is very likely to be met or nudged up. The 10% risk of a reduction is concentrated at the 12 November 2026 results and is more likely to come from the cash line than from profit. The November 2027 results are the widest event. 'Softened' medium-term targets means targets that are re-dated or re-weighted.

Evidence: consensus. FY2027 EPS consensus will probably drift up 1% to 3% as the four brokers who published before the October update book 'upper end' and the buyback. FY2028 consensus is more likely to hold than to move: the model's organic like-for-like gap is only +1% to +3%, and the brokers already model a 1.6T ramp. FY2029 consensus can move either way: +2% to +4% with a first bolt-on acquisition, or down 5% to 8% on FY2028 and 10% on FY2029 in the renewal-loss branch.

EBITDA is the line most likely to be revised up, because consensus depreciation and amortisation of 37.7m to 42.6m sits well below capital expenditure of 50m to 56m and ignores KST's assets. A cut within 18 months requires the renewal to go wrong, which has a probability of about 25%, concentrated at November 2027.

Evidence: narrative. The narrative shift available is from 'AI beneficiary whose growth is slowing' to 'compounder whose EPS grows faster than its revenue, with cash coming back'. The 12 November results can start the shift (cash conversion, the data-centre split), and the June 2027 results can confirm it (FY2027 EPS of 0.53 to 0.545, working capital near 26.5%). The novel positives that would re-rate the shares rather than defend them (a disclosed multi-year data-centre commitment, a sizeable accretive acquisition, a visible cash release) have no dates.

Inference. The scope for upgrades is modest and mostly mechanical, and the two active brokers have already pre-empted part of it. A narrative upgrade is possible, but it would be a re-anchoring from a label to a record, which defends a multiple rather than lifting it. Against a top-decile trailing multiple, a known sequence of events is unlikely to lift the shares much until the trailing-P/E optics unwind in June 2027.

So what. Richard's test asks for an unusually positive skew in the probability of guidance and sell-side upgrades. Over six to twelve months Volex does not pass it: the skew is balanced to slightly positive on FY2027 and cash, neutral on FY2028, and carries a 25% risk of a cut at the eighteen-month mark.

Counter-case. Three things could produce an unexpected upgrade cycle: a bolt-on acquisition (the pipeline is 'larger than historic averages', and the balance sheet can take 200m); a January 2027 trading update on the FY2026 pattern; and a positive surprise in H1 cash, if hub stock was drawn down as data-centre revenue fell. The breadth of the October revisions (EPS, EBITDA, sales and target prices all up across six brokers) shows that the upgrade machinery works when it is given a reason.

What would raise my view

  • Any of the three counter-case events
  • The active brokers' FY2028 revenue moving up toward the median

What would lower my view

  • H1 working capital above 28% of trailing revenue
  • Any H2 data-centre commentary softer than 'below H2 FY2026'

Market versus my view. The narrative report's view that 'further raises are the most probable outcome' is right for FY2027 and unsupported for FY2028. The brokers' targets of 730p to 750p (+25% to +30%) mean they need no estimate change to stay at Buy, so the risk is drift rather than downgrade.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The scope is small. Guidance is likely to be met or nudged up (about 85%), and FY2027 consensus EPS should drift up 1% to 3%; against 9% to 15% revenue growth, that is a ratio of only about 0.1 to 0.2. EBITDA is the line likelier to rise, and FY2028 is held at best. The 25% risk of a cut on the renewal falls at November 2027, at the edge of the window, and the narrative can re-anchor to 'compounder' but has no dated catalyst. The score is slightly below the peer group's 54 because of that cut risk, between Spie's modest plausible raise and Kerry's stuck narrative.

#8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: momentum in guidance, revisions and narrative is still positive but late-stage, and it will decay by January on arithmetic alone. Technical momentum is intact on the long trend and broken on the short. The shares' rising beta to the data-centre theme means that sector news now moves them more than company news does.

Evidence: guidance and sell-side. Guidance was raised to 'upper end' on 19 October. FY2027 consensus has risen steeply over twelve months but only marginally over one month (chart). The consensus target price has moved 0%, +8% and +26% over the reported windows. The buy share is 86%, up 14 points over three months (five Buys, one restricted Hold, no Sell). The dashboard's sell-side momentum grade is A (29 October), with a revision-momentum score of 14.

One-month revisions in the low single digits mark a late-stage cycle. By late January the three-month window will contain only the November results, so the three-month revision figure will fall to the low single digits, and the dashboard's grade will fall with it, without any estimate being cut.

Evidence: narrative. The broker narrative is uniform and optimistic. Zeus calls a calendar-2027 P/E of 14.3x 'undemanding' against BizLink at about 30x and a historical peak of 20x; Jefferies says data-centre exposure is 'not factored into trading multiples'. No broker document carries a contrary view, and there is no Twitter, forum or fund-letter commentary. For a 1.4bn USD stock, that silence says the shareholder register is UK institutions following the two active brokers (Investec Wealth 4.7%, Octopus 4.7%, Rathbones 4.2%, Fidelity 3.3%, abrdn 2.3%, Ruffer 2.1%), plus passive FTSE 250 holders since September.

Share-price behaviour tells a different story. The shares fell about 6% on 15 October, alongside Huber+Suhner's 56% fall in communication orders, and 7% on 23 October in a rotation out of AI names (Deutsche Bank). The co-movement figures below confirm that the market now trades Volex with the data-centre theme. No significant short interest is recorded.

Evidence: technicals. The long trend is intact, but the price has broken below its shorter averages.

Evidence: peers. Primary suppliers are being upgraded: Amphenol's FY2027 EPS by 11% at Rothschild Redburn; TE's FY2027 estimates on AI orders up 70%; BizLink's FY2027 net profit forecast up 64%; and Luxshare's EPS forecast to compound at 33% a year to 2028. Volex's dashboard profile (technical B, sell-side A, valuation F) matches AQ Group's.

Inference. Momentum is positive on every series and late on every series. Guidance momentum has moved from 'raised' to 'upper end'. Sell-side momentum is at its mechanical peak. The narrative is unanimous, which is a risk rather than a comfort, because the first downgrade from a uniformly positive base becomes the perception event. Technical momentum is intact on the 200-day average and broken on the 50-day. The market trades the shares as a high-beta expression of the European data-centre theme: in a risk-off market a 10% fall in the basket maps to about an 18% fall in Volex, before any company news.

So what. The momentum that is still improving lies in fundamentals the market is not watching (cash and below-the-line EPS), not in the series the dashboard scores. Read the dashboard's three letters accordingly:

Counter-case. The sector's upgrades (Amphenol, TE, BizLink, Luxshare) are a necessary condition for Volex's level of demand, and they are all positive. BizLink's monthly sales (+39% in September) are the highest-frequency read on the sector, and they are accelerating. A January trading update on the FY2026 pattern would restart the revision series.

What would raise my view

  • A January trading update
  • The price reclaiming its 50-day average with the H1 results
  • BizLink's monthly sales staying above +30%

What would lower my view

  • The first broker downgrade
  • Huber+Suhner's Q4 orders (January) staying weak
  • Credit stress in the AI complex widening

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures are in the top fifth. Guidance was raised to 'upper end' in October, FY2027 EPS consensus is up 14% over three months and 35% over twelve, the buy share is 86%, and primary-supplier peers are being upgraded, so no part is outright negative and the letter is A. The number sits at the floor of the band: revisions are late-stage (+2% over one month) and will decay by January on arithmetic alone, the price is below its 50-day average, and the six-month return is -10.8% against the basket.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

Conclusion: the case is simple to state (one open driver, two decided ones) but hard to track, because the open driver is undisclosed, customer-controlled and reported only half-yearly. The case has a fat left tail in which earnings, hub inventory and the multiple fall together, which is why I rate its riskiness D despite the predictability of FY2027.

Simplicity of the case and its drivers. Three drivers generate almost the whole difference between the forecasts and the last five years. Everything management controls (self-help, pricing, mix, acquisitions) changes the numbers by only tenths of a point a year. That concentration makes EPS and cash more predictable than the revenue line suggests. It also makes the range of outcomes around FY2028 wider than a model with many small drivers would produce, because the only open driver is one undisclosed account that the customer controls.

Fragilities, assumptions and requirements. About three-quarters of the thesis rests on demonstrated strengths, and one-quarter on three things the company has not yet shown.

The evidence on each of the three untested requirements is cautionary:

  • Holding a secondary hyperscale allocation through a technology transition. Volex's own 400G rollout in FY2021 to FY2022 was delayed by certification while Amphenol and Luxshare qualified first. Luxshare became a primary supplier only after building optical and 224G capability, which Volex lacks.
  • Releasing hub stock as cash without write-downs. The contract puts obsolescence risk on the customer, but Jabil's excess-and-obsolete reserve rose from 67m to 87m as cloud volumes plateaued, Celestica warns that it 'may not be fully reimbursed', Flex's hyperscale customers can terminate for convenience, and PwC flags Volex's inventory provisioning.
  • Converting an enlarged acquisition pipeline at the company's own discipline. Volex went two years without a deal before KST.

Other fragilities: two customers account for 29.9% of revenue, and the largest for 16.2% of trade receivables; the peso is unhedged (a 20% surge costs about 14 cents of EPS without pricing action); Turkish tax de-indexation runs to 2027, alongside lira volatility; a breakdown of USMCA is unlikely but would be costly; there is key-person risk with no disclosed successor, and the chair holds a second executive role; and recurring restructuring (3m to 4m a year) and share-based payments (7m) are excluded from underlying profit.

How share-price risks arrive: suddenly, through peers, and all at once. Data-centre news arrives suddenly, through trading updates. Volex reports half-yearly, with no order data, no data-centre segment, no contract tenure and no hub balance, which puts it at the thin end of its peer group on the one dimension that matters: AQ Group reports quarterly with orders, discoverIE discloses a bank of design wins, and BizLink reports monthly sales.

Perception risks arrive through peers (Huber+Suhner on 15 October) and through the theme (23 October), and they arrive often: hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance and Amphenol's and TE's quarterly results in late January; Credo's results in early December and early March; OFC (7 to 11 March 2027) and Nvidia GTC (14 to 18 March 2027); and BizLink's sales every month. The three main risks (revenue, hub inventory and the multiple) share one cause and would arrive together. A diligent analyst can track them from outside through these external series, but the company's own disclosure confirms or refutes the thesis one half-year after the fact.

Sector and cyclical precedents. The precedents show a consistent pattern. Diversified assemblers come through, but a single-customer line produces at least one sharp correction within four to six quarters of its peak, and the correction arrives before the disclosure. Restocking pulses run for six to eighteen months. Volex's data-centre revenue peaked in H2 FY2026 and had its first sequential decline in H1 FY2027, so a second leg down, if there is one, would show between H2 FY2027 and H1 FY2028.

How far could the shares fall? On the model's two-year-forward EPS at September 2027 (about 0.77), a 10x trough multiple gives about 580p, today's price, and 9x gives about 525p. In the renewal-loss branch (EPS about 10% lower, at 0.70), 10x gives about 525p (-11%) and 9x about 470p (-20%). In the design-loss branch (EPS 20% lower, at 0.62, plus a write-down), 9x gives about 420p (-29%). Jefferies' published downside is 465p to 490p.

The multiple is driven by the company: it rose with the margin and the AI label, and fell on the company's own update. A de-rating would therefore most likely coincide with an earnings disappointment rather than precede it. The compression since mid-October, from 14.1x to about 12.3x, has already covered about half the distance to a 10x trough.

Market versus my view. The brokers' dispersion (FY2027 revenue within plus or minus 2%; FY2029 EPS within plus or minus 5%) measures their agreement about the open driver, not the driver's range of outcomes; only Jefferies' downside scenario treats the driver as open. I treat it as the case's defining risk.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. FY2027 is predictable to about 4%, and leverage is low (1.0x). But FY2028 EPS ranges from -12% to +8%, skewed down, on one undisclosed, customer-controlled account at renewal through a technology transition. Earnings, hub inventory and the multiple would fall together, the shares carry a 1.77 beta to the data-centre theme, and reporting is half-yearly with no order data. The score sits between the two risk peer groups (32 and 53): below Rexel's leveraged but diffuse cyclicality, and above D'Ieteren's guided 40% profit fall in a complex holding company.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is stalling after a phase in which its thesis broadened, while the business underneath keeps broadening. The phase will resolve toward 'reinforcing as a compounder' or 'collapsing on one account' on evidence that the company itself supplies on 12 November 2026 and in November 2027.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the 'Broadening' phase. The evidence for 'broadening' and for 'stalling' is set out below. For 'collapsing' there is no evidence yet: no estimate cut, no deterioration in management and no reported revenue decline. For 'reinforcing', the compounder narrative (cash back, margin up, bolt-ons) is available but unproven.

Inference. The business is broadening; the stock is stalling. The market's thesis (AI beneficiary) has stalled and is partly priced. The company's thesis (broad compounder) is intact but has not yet earned its own multiple. The company, not the sector, decides the next phase, at the 12 November 2026 results (cash and the data-centre split) and the November 2027 results (renewals and the 1.6T ramp). The Analyst's probabilities for the stock's state in twelve months are: reinforcing as a compounder about 50%; still stalling about 30%; collapsing on a renewal loss about 20%.

So what. A stalling phase argues for a fair multiple at or below the guideline, and for buying on the company's evidence rather than the sector's. It also means that the 'reinforcing' outcome, if it comes, starts from a price that already discounts the plateau, and that is the attraction.

Counter-case. The dashboard's rule may be right that Volex is still broadening: EPS growth of +23% and then +15% is not a stalling profile, the 200-day trend is unbroken, and the October fall could prove to be a correction within a broadening phase rather than its end.

What would move the stock toward 'reinforcing'

  • Working capital falling at the H1 results
  • A bolt-on acquisition
  • An 'in line' FY2028 outlook in June 2027, with data-centre revenue flat

What would move the stock toward 'collapsing'

  • A renewal concession visible in the H2 FY2027 margin or the November 2027 results
  • BizLink's sales decelerating sharply
  • A write-down of hub inventory

Market versus my view. The dashboard says 'broadening', and the brokers say 'normalising before the next ramp'. I say the market's thesis is stalling and the business is broadening, with the company holding the decision.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The business is broadening (five segments growing, margin rising, EPS compounding at about 13%), but the stock has stalled. The AI thesis has plateaued, organic growth falls from about 21% in H1 to 3% to 5% in H2, sell-side momentum is at its mechanical peak, and the price is below its 50-day average. The memo gives 50% to reinforcing as a compounder, 30% to stalling and 20% to collapsing. The multiple has already reset from 14.1x to 12.3x, which makes this a better point of entry than BP's late 'Reinforcing' phase at a commodity peak, but a less attractive one than Greggs' early 'Turning' phase.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline 12.57x is a reasonable twelve-month fair multiple, which I would set a touch lower (a range of 12.0x to 12.6x, central 12.0x) while the stock is stalling and cash conversion is unproven. At about 12.3x the shares are therefore already at fair value, and the return has to come from earnings.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the 'Broadening' phase is 12.57x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history. The ten-year bands are: 10th percentile 7.5x ('crash'), median 10.2x ('prudent'), 75th percentile 12.1x ('defendable') and 90th percentile 14.0x ('mania'). The five-year median is 10.9x, and the 2021 peak was about 19x to 20x. On consensus EPS the dashboard's two-year-forward multiple is 14.47x; on the model's EPS at 590p the stock trades at about 12.3x, 2% below the guideline.

The case for a multiple in the upper half of the history

The history was earned mostly by a business with 2% to 9% margins. Today's 10% to 11% margin, 20% ROCE, rising cash conversion and 13% to 15% EPS compounding deserve the upper half.

Peers carrying the AI label trade far higher (BizLink at about 30x forward earnings, SINBON at about 17x), and discoverIE trades at about 17x trailing earnings. UK industrials trade about 30% below continental peers, and private equity is closing the gap.

Volex's EPS is more robust than its revenue, because the EPS growth comes from below the line.

The case for a multiple below the guideline

The phase is closer to stalling than broadening, and Richard's rule sets the multiple lower where forecasts are more uncertain.

The fastest-growing revenue is the least protected: short contracts, one hyperscaler, build-to-specification, funded by working capital. The market's template is Halma's Avo Photonics, valued at 10x to 13x EBITA against about 22x for Halma's core; applied to Volex, the data-centre fifth of revenue deserves a discount to the certified half.

A 1.77 beta to a theme in a risk-off market argues for a margin of safety, and 64% cash conversion is not a premium-multiple number until it recovers.

My view. A fair range of 12.0x to 12.6x two-year-forward earnings for the next twelve months. The central figure is 12.0x (the 'defendable' 75th percentile) while the stock is stalling and cash conversion is unproven, rising to the guideline 12.57x once the H1 results show working capital falling and data-centre revenue holds through H1 FY2028. The trough multiple is 10x (the renewal-loss branch) and the peak 14x (a 1.6T win plus acquisitions).

The gap between 12.0x and the guideline is only about 4% to 5% of value, so I accept the guideline as a reasonable twelve-month anchor rather than a generous one. At 590p the shares already sit in my fair range, so the multiple is roughly right now. The mispricing is in the optics of the trailing P/E (14.5x, 92nd percentile, the dashboard's F), which unwind as FY2027 earnings enter the trailing base in June 2027.

Market versus my view. The brokers' targets (730p to 750p) imply 15x to 16x their FY2028 EPS, which is the BizLink-and-SINBON argument; the dashboard's F implies the stock is expensive. I agree with neither: the stock is fairly priced on forward earnings, cheap against theme peers, and expensive only on trailing optics.

Score: 22, set by the Rater. Dear on both measures, so the letter is F. The number sits at the top of the band because the readings partly overstate the dearness: on the model's two-year-forward EPS the stock trades at about 12.3x, around the 75th to 80th percentile of its history (75th percentile 12.1x), and a margin that has risen from 2%-9% to 10%-11% earns some premium over the company's own past. A stalling phase argues against more than that.

#12Total shareholder return at the guideline fair multiple

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the shares offer about +24% to September 2027 and about +51% to March 2029 from 590p (about four points less on the cross-check EPS). Almost all of that return comes from earnings growth, which is two-thirds revenue, a quarter margin and an eighth flat interest. The multiple contributes about 2%, and the left tail (-10% to -30%) sits in one account.

The model's return, at its 545p starting price of 22 October. At 545p the two-year-forward P/E was 11.4x, against the guideline 12.57x reached at the 18-month column. On that basis the value at 30 September 2027 is 7.31 GBP and the value at 31 March 2029 is 8.73 GBP. The multiple and earnings parts multiply, and dividends add. The horizons are the model's fixed columns, so September 2027 is eleven months from today and March 2029 is twenty-eight months away.

Re-based to 590p (29 October), which the Financial Analyst has not yet done. The target values stay unchanged (fair multiple times forward EPS), so the higher starting price does the work.

To 30 September 2027 (11 months)

about +24%

7.31 GBP from 5.90 GBP is +23.9% in price, plus about 0.9% of dividends: about +26% annualised.

To 31 March 2029 (28 months)

about +51%

8.73 GBP from 5.90 GBP is +48% in price, plus about 3% of dividends: about +19% annualised.

At 590p the two-year-forward P/E is about 12.3x, so the multiple leg shrinks from +10.4% to about +2% (12.3x to 12.57x). The earnings leg stays at +20.7% to September 2027 and +42.3% to March 2029, and dividends at +0.9% and +3.0% (a yield under 1%).

What drives the earnings leg. Today's two-year-forward EPS is the model's FY2028 figure of 0.64. At September 2027 the two-year-forward EPS becomes the FY2029-to-FY2030 blend of about 0.77 (+21%); at March 2029 it becomes FY2031's 0.91 (+42%). Decomposing the +42% from FY2028 to FY2031: revenue growth of +28% supplies about two-thirds (5.5% to 6% organic growth, plus KST and about 175m of acquired revenue); the margin rise from 11.1% to 11.9% supplies about a quarter; and flat interest while profit grows supplies about an eighth; tax and the share count are flat. Acquisitions contribute about 6% of FY2031 EPS (0.873 against 0.823 on the cross-check), so without them the three-year earnings leg is about +34% and TSR about +42%.

The honest range for the base case is +19% to +24% over eleven months and +45% to +51% over twenty-eight months. The model's EPS is basic and before minorities, about 4% above the Analyst's cross-check (0.64 against 0.614 for FY2028), and about four points above a like-for-like comparison with diluted consensus. On the cross-check basis the September 2027 value is about 7.0 GBP and TSR about +19%, and TSR to March 2029 is about +45%.

The branches, on the same basis.

  • Renewal loss (FY2029 EPS about 10% lower) at a 10x trough: about 525p, -11% in price (-10% TSR).
  • Design loss (EPS 20% lower, plus a write-down) at 9x: about 420p, -29%.
  • 1.6T win plus acquisitions to plan (EPS 5% to 10% higher) at 14x: about 840p to 880p, +42% to +49%.
  • Working capital back to 24%: no EPS effect, but 'cash back' is what would lift the multiple from 12x toward 14x, worth about 15%.

Market versus my view. The brokers' 730p to 750p targets (+25% to +30%) are close to the model's September 2027 value, but the brokers reach it on a higher multiple and lower EPS. I reach a similar place by a different route (earnings, not re-rating), and I attach a fatter left tail.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Weighting the memo's branches gives about +20% to +25% over 18 months, almost all from earnings, and the three-year check (about 17% to 19% a year) agrees. The number is placed just above the 75 that +20% would earn rather than at the 77 for +22%, because the left tail (-10% to -30%, concentrated in one account) is fatter than the right, and the memo's own central multiple is a touch below the guideline.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Volex is a good business run by an exceptional owner-operator, midway through changing its story from 'UK AI-infrastructure play' to 'broad-based compounder with one exposed line'. The market has priced the first half of that change: the share price is down a fifth from its mid-October high, and the forward multiple is back in the defendable band. The market has not yet noticed the second half: EPS now compounds at 13% to 15% while revenue grows at about 9%, because the interest, tax and dilution that took about ten points a year off EPS growth from FY2022 to FY2026 have stopped.

FY2027 is nearly locked, at about 155m of operating profit and EPS of 0.535 to 0.55, with the H2 margin the one fragile number. FY2028 depends on one account: the largest customer (about 18.7% of revenue, in effect the whole data-centre line), at renewal through the 1.6T transition, where the downside is larger than the upside. A 25% loss of that account takes FY2029 EPS to consensus, and a halving takes it 20% below the model. Cash is the swing factor, and 12 November is its first test: if working capital falls as the hub build stops, the compounder narrative gets a runway to June 2027; if it does not, the narrative turns to cash even while profit beats.

At 590p the shares trade at about 12.3x the model's two-year-forward EPS, against a guideline fair multiple of 12.57x that I would set a touch lower while the stock is stalling. The multiple therefore neither helps nor much hinders, and the return at the guideline is about +24% to September 2027 and about +51% to March 2029, nearly all from earnings. That is a decent, earnings-driven return with a fat left tail, and no upgrade cycle will carry it until an acquisition or a 1.6T allocation gives the brokers a reason.

On Richard's test, the skew is balanced today rather than unusually positive. It becomes unusually positive if the shares fall toward 500p on sector noise without company news, or if the 12 November results show cash coming back and the data-centre share of CIT restated. Either event would put the company-controlled three-quarters of the thesis on sale at a price that already discounts the customer-controlled quarter.
